result:
Opening a DB connection is expensive: TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication, server-side session setup (Postgres forks a whole backend process per connection). Doing that per request → tens of ms of latency added to queries that take 1 ms, plus heavy server load. Pool fix: open N connections once, keep them alive, lend them out. App calls `getConnection()` → pool hands over an idle one; app "closes" it → pool resets session state and marks it idle, socket stays open. All connections busy → caller waits in a queue (with timeout) or pool grows up to a max.

Why it helps beyond latency: it caps concurrency. DBs degrade badly with too many simultaneous connections (memory per connection, lock contention, context switching), so a pool of ~10–50 often outperforms 500 direct connections, since requests queue cheaply in the app instead of thrashing the DB. Rule of thumb for sizing: roughly `cores * 2` plus spindles/IO headroom, then measure. Pools also handle health checks (validate before lending, evict dead connections after DB restarts or firewall idle timeouts), max lifetime (recycle to avoid stale state/leaks), and min-idle warm connections.

Two placements: in-process (HikariCP, SQLAlchemy pool, pgx pool), which is per app instance, so total connections = instances × pool size, a common way to exhaust `max_connections` when autoscaling; or external proxy (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy), which multiplexes many app connections onto few DB connections. PgBouncer in transaction mode is most efficient but breaks session-scoped features (prepared statements in older setups, `SET`, advisory locks, temp tables). Gotchas: leaked connections (never returned → pool starves, fix with try/finally or context managers), long transactions holding connections, and serverless functions each creating their own pool → use an external proxy there.
